title: Verdicts Expire With The Bytes; Decisions Are Priced

intelligence.essence: Every verdict is a function of the bytes it was computed on, and every "wait" is a purchase that must be priced. A repair built on a moved tip silently becomes a second defect — two commits of lag is a different world (SN-745). A verdict *survives* a tip move only transitively, when the exact blob it was computed on is byte-identical at both tips and both SHAs are cited (SN-727). A stand-down is earned only after currency re-verification — the RED still reproduces, the claimed head actually fixes it, the repaired files are byte-identical between claim base and tip (SN-716) — and coverage is proven, not assumed: a lane that stood down assuming a wave covered its instances grepped the wave's patches, found zero mentions, overturned its own disposition in public, and built the repair itself (SN-776). A CI job that dies before the check runs yields UNKNOWN, not a verdict (SN-694). A superseded run that leaves no receipt is indistinguishable from a swallowed failure (SN-723). And in any scorecard, a wait option is priced on information gain: if the future cannot return a verdict the present cannot — the check fails identically on the base, or the environment cannot produce the evidence at all — the wait is worth ~0 minus indefinite delay (SN-798, SN-755).
intelligence.human_view: A decision made yesterday about files that changed overnight is a decision about a world that no longer exists. This essence is about keeping decisions attached to reality: check that the fix still matches the current code before merging it, check that the person you deferred to is actually handling your problem — by reading their work, not assuming — and when someone proposes "let's wait for more information," ask the only question that matters: what could the future possibly tell us that we can't already know? If the answer is nothing — the test is broken in the same way everywhere, the camera literally cannot take that picture here — then waiting isn't caution. It's just delay wearing caution's clothes.
intelligence.child_view: Imagine you draw a map of your classroom, then the teacher rearranges all the desks. Your map isn't wrong because you drew it badly — it's wrong because the room changed. You need a new map, unless the one corner you care about stayed exactly the same — then you can point and say, "that corner didn't move, so that part of my map still works." And imagine a friend says, "I'll tell you tomorrow if your drawing is good, after I ask my broken camera." If the camera is broken today and broken tomorrow, waiting for it tells you nothing. Decide with the eyes you have.
intelligence.grandma_view: Dear, it's the wisdom of checking the larder before you cook from last week's list, and of not putting off a decision for news that cannot come. If the road report you need comes from a bridge that's washed out, you don't wait by the river — you take the sound road and note why. And when you hand a job to someone, you look in on the work itself, not just the promise; if the promised helper never had your parcel, the honest thing is to say so out loud and carry it yourself.
intelligence.ai_view: Anchor every verdict to the bytes it was computed on, and re-anchor explicitly: byte-identical blob + both SHAs, or the verdict expired (SN-727, SN-745). Earn your stand-downs with the currency receipt — reproduce, verify the claim head, compare the bytes (SN-716) — and prove coverage from the wave's own patches before you assume it (SN-776). Read steps, not job badges; when the check never ran, write UNKNOWN (SN-694). Make even your refused runs leave receipts (SN-723). And in every scorecard, price the wait: name the instrument, test producibility, classify predetermined checks instead of gating on them (SN-798, SN-755).
intelligence.what_it_means: Eight notes are one law in two halves: **currency** and **pricing**. Currency: a verdict, a repair, a stand-down, and a coverage assumption are all claims about the present state of a moving repository, and each note installs the mechanical re-check that keeps the claim present-tense — blob identity (SN-727), tip re-derivation (SN-745), the three-part receipt (SN-716), the patch grep (SN-776), step enumeration (SN-694), the durable race receipt (SN-723). Pricing: once the present is known, the remaining question — act or wait — is arithmetic, not temperament: the wait is worth exactly the information it can return (SN-798), and a gate demanding unproducible evidence is not rigor but a permanent block (SN-755). A cold reader holding only this essence can still audit any merge decision in the system: what bytes, what tip, what could waiting have taught us?
whats_inside: Repairs are valid only against the tip they were built on; re-derive the base and diff the covered delta before merge (SN-745).
Verdicts transfer across a tip move only via a named, byte-identical evidence blob, citing both SHAs (SN-727).
Stand-downs are earned by a three-part currency receipt (RED reproduces, claim head fixes, files byte-identical) — never by deference to an open claim (SN-716).

Assumed wave coverage is falsifiable and must be falsified or proven: registered scope list + patch grep; a falsified stand-down is overturned publicly by its own lane, which then builds scope-disjoint (SN-776).
Job outcomes are summaries; step-level enumeration decides, and a job that dies before the check yields UNKNOWN (SN-694).
Superseded runs must still emit receipts; silence is the defect even when the refusal is correct (SN-723).
Wait options are priced on information gain; predetermined checks are classifications, not gates; unproducible-evidence waits score ~0 (SN-798, SN-755).
